title: Clo User Story - Annboo
description:
Meet Anbo, founder of ANNBOO and a 10-year CLO user. For his team, more than 60% of product development is completely digitized. By previewing silhouettes, proportions, and fabric drape in 3D, they've drastically reduced sampling time and costs, especially for their complex new line of pet-owner matching outfits! 🐶👕

Ready to level up your workflow? Discover how Anbo is using CLO to demystify complex pattern-making and let brilliant ideas reach reality faster.

markdown_content: ## Overview: Anbo’s Work with CLO (Clover) This section introduces Anbo and her role teaching CLO at Huazhong University of Taiwan and East China University of China, plus her long-term experience using CLO in design workflows. It also frames CLO as a key tool for modeling, rendering, and improving creative development efficiency. Anbo is a fashion designer and a senior educator who teaches CLO at Huazhong University of Taiwan and East China University of China. She first began using CLO about 16 years ago. In her workflow, CLO supports collaboration between designers and teams that build garments: the team models the clothes first, checks results, and iterates based on the designer’s direction. Anbo emphasizes that CLO’s usefulness is closely tied to software updates. After CLO was updated to version 6.0, the rendering effect improved significantly, which made it easier to evaluate design outcomes during development. ## CLO Rendering and Iteration (Including v6.0 Improvements) This section explains how CLO’s rendering improvements and modeling tools support faster evaluation of garment design details, especially during intensive development periods. Anbo describes situations where the team was “in a hurry” and it was inconvenient to go out. During these development sessions, communication with the designer was critical, and they often had to test outcomes using their own software rather than relying on external production steps. With CLO version 6.0, they observed a major improvement in rendering quality. This helped the team evaluate the “results” more effectively during early development and reduced friction between design intent and what could be visualized. ## 3D Virtual Fashion Shows: Using CLO for Fashion Week Participation This section covers how Anbo’s team created a 3D virtual fashion show using CLO to participate in major fashion events, including China’s World Fashion Week and Shenzhen’s Fashion Week. Anbo notes that CLO also enabled their production of a 3D virtual fashion show. They used CLO to develop and present designs in a way suitable for participation in China’s World Fashion Week and Shenzhen’s Fashion Week. She frames CLO as a tool that helps address early “achievements of creative design” by making design concepts more visible and testable before physical prototyping and production. ## Traditional Production vs. 3D Workflow (Efficiency Gains) This section contrasts traditional fashion production steps with 3D modeling in CLO, highlighting how CLO helps designers validate outlines, proportions, and craftsmanship details earlier. In the traditional production process, teams must proceed through platform steps and test “white cloth” (early fabric/prototype testing). In CLO, designers can quickly view the outline of garments and evaluate proportions, positions, and craftsmanship details directly in the 3D environment. CLO also supports examining how different fabrics, colors, and textures combine visually. Anbo stresses that seeing these visual effects in 3D goes beyond traditional fashion design approaches and substantially improves designer efficiency. ## Award-Winning Project (2022) and 3D Modeling Deliverables This section details Anbo’s 2022 award recognition and the specific use of 3D modeling to present men’s design concepts and environmental models for thematic emphasis. In 2022, Anbo won the Qipilang China Fashion Crafts Creative Design Award. For this project, the team used 3D modeling to create a series of men’s designs intended to suggest a brand direction. Anbo highlights that CLO allowed them to present style details objectively. While building the designs, they also created environmental models in 3D, which helped better highlight the theme of their designs. ## Daily CLO Usage: Modeling Proportions and Applying Real Fabric This section describes how CLO is used in day-to-day development, including the proportion adjustment loop and the workflow that transitions from 3D visualization to real fabric. Anbo states that CLO is very important in daily design development. More than 60% of their 3D models are modeled in CLO. The workflow typically follows this pattern: - Model in CLO and “look at the effect” - Adjust proportions as needed - Then use real fabric to achieve the intended design outcome (“use the real fabric to make the sincerity,” i.e., faithful realization) She presents CLO as a practical tool for refining design decisions before committing to physical materials. ## Pet and Adult Family Makeup Series: From 3D Modeling to Conversion This section explains how Anbo’s team handles the pet and adult family makeup series by using CLO for 3D modeling first, then converting the models into “food” (as described in the transcript). It includes the general approach for evaluating approximate effects. Anbo mentions that this year they developed a “pet and adult family makeup series.” For pet makeup, they typically: - Perform 3D modeling and modeling in CLO - Check approximate effects in 3D - Convert these models into “food” (as stated) ## Skills Required: Fashion Sensitivity, Design Taste, Pattern Making, and Sewing Understanding This section lists the personal and technical abilities Anbo believes designers need to move from fashion ideas to patterns and finally to real clothing, including board ability, size/proportion understanding, fabric handling, and sewing process knowledge. Anbo emphasizes that to succeed in this workflow, you must: 1. Be very interested in fashion and sensitive to it. 2. Have good taste in design. 3. Put the thoughts and ideas of the designs on drawing paper. 4. Convert those ideas into a specific pattern and actual clothes. She adds that designers need strong “board ability” (pattern-related ability) and a clear understanding of size and proportion. In the transition to real garments, designers must also have: - Strong fabric handling ability - Understanding of the entire sewing process ## Best Practice: Build the Desired Look in 3D (CLO) Before Physical Production This section provides guidance on using 3D modeling to closely match real-world results, including the recommendation to use 3D (and more specificity) when a 4D workflow is not possible. Anbo recommends putting a dress into CLO to create the effect they want, aiming to make it as close to the real effect as possible. If you cannot achieve the desired accuracy in “4D,” she suggests using 3D modeling and making it more specific to improve fidelity. She also describes the general approach of creating a 3D model within the software, checking the model, and presenting results—positioning CLO as the central environment for evaluation and iteration.
